Additional file 1

How accurate is altitude from pressure geolocators? Supplementary methods and results

Author

Raphaël Nussbaumer, Mathieu Gravey

This supplement provides reference-data rules and full-height error summaries (S1), environmental profiles (S2), the ERA5 product comparison (S3), reference-height and weighting checks (S4), and a horizontal-position pilot (S5). It uses the main manuscript’s three conversions and error definitions: error is estimated minus reference height; station bias is mean signed error; SD is within-station variability; and p95 is the 95th percentile of individual absolute errors. ERA5 standard denotes the ERA5 surface reference with the standard lapse rate; ERA5 virtual + GPT3 adds virtual temperature and a climatological lapse rate. Code, input provenance and extended diagnostics accompany the analysis [1].

S1 Reference data, selection and error distributions

Reference data and matching

GHCNh supplies ground pressure and reported station elevation for each station’s latest qualifying year in 2022–2026 [2]. HadISD locations define the initial candidate footprint only. One randomly selected station per 2° cell is supplemented by stations above 1000 m; after screening, each retained cell receives equal weight, divided among its stations. GNSS barometers provide a complementary ground check in 2022–2024 [3, 4], and IGRA2 soundings provide the flight-height reference in 2023–2024 [5–7]. MeteoSwiss methods and results are in S4. Missing reference observations are not filled.

All observations are matched to ERA5 single-level surface pressure, 2 m temperature, dewpoint and orography at the nearest 0.25° grid cell and hour [8, 9]. GHCNh reports use the nearest hour (half-hour ties go to the earlier hour), retaining the first report per hour. GNSS samples within ±1 min of an hour are averaged to unique station-hours. Radiosonde level times combine release and elapsed ascent times; missing values use nominal release time or a 5 m s\(^{-1}\) ascent estimate. All levels use launch-station coordinates, ignoring balloon drift.

IGRA2 reports geopotential heights; these do not establish independent geometric-height accuracy at every level. We retain levels 1–6000 m above each sounding’s surface, substituting station elevation if surface height is missing. Source extraction requires pressure \(\geq 400\) hPa, so vertical coverage also depends on launch elevation. Table 4 gives support by height band; no additional station filter is applied within bands.

Selection and quality control

Table 1 gives the retained rules. Listed station elevation may differ from barometer height [10, 11], and the ERA5-residual-based screen cannot distinguish reference errors from model errors. Screened ground results are therefore conditional on selection; S4 tests its effect. The step check uses monthly medians from the selected year and up to two preceding years, with a month-of-year effect and one breakpoint. It requires at least 18 monthly medians spanning all 12 calendar months: 2023 of 2144 post-match coverage-qualified stations were testable. Other stations are untested, rather than demonstrated stable.

GNSS heights combine site-log marker/antenna heights and barometer offsets; EGM96 geoid undulation is subtracted from ellipsoidal heights. The median signed difference from the file-header height must be within ±1 m. This checks metadata consistency, without establishing metre-level absolute accuracy or independence from ERA5. Retained ground coverage is summarized in Table 2; partial 2026 records must pass the same reporting threshold as completed years (S4).

Individual errors across the three conversions

Table 3 and Table 4 extend the main Results with individual-error distributions. Ground observation weights divide each station’s spatial weight among its retained hours. Flight weights divide each station’s weight among all retained levels, then normalize within each height band. All conversions use identical observations and weights. Flight errors subtract the same sounding’s surface error and exclude absolute ground-reference offsets.

S2 How the error varies

Ground: elevation gap, climate and time

The station–ERA5 elevation gap is associated with within-station scatter (Figure 1): fitted SD rises from 3.2 m at zero gap to 11.2 m at a 1000 m gap. This gap is distinct from terrain roughness, the sub-grid SD of orography used to classify terrain in the main manuscript. Seasonal, local-time and climate profiles provide context for the pooled ground summaries (Figure 2; Figure 3); the polar group has greater scatter.

Only 5 stations contribute to the paired historical comparison (Figure 4). Their discrepancies decline across the sampled years, but this small common-station subset cannot establish a global accuracy trend.

Flight: climate, season and column temperature

Climate and half-year profiles show why a pooled signed error can conceal opposing biases (Figure 5). The corrected conversion reduces these seasonal biases, while a climatological lapse rate cannot reproduce every sounding’s profile. For ERA5 standard, the error predicted from the assumed versus observed mean column temperature closely follows the surface-referenced error (r = 0.97; Figure 6). Night-time underestimation is generally greater than daytime underestimation (Figure 7), consistent with surface inversions making the column warmer than the surface-based profile assumes.

S3 ERA5 single-levels and ERA5-Land

ERA5-Land’s finer 0.1° grid [12] does not reduce persistent ground offsets in these comparisons. Median station |bias| is 9.9 m versus 2.9 m for ERA5 single-levels at GHCNh stations, with the same ordering at GNSS and MeteoSwiss stations (Figure 8). Surface-referenced flight errors are similar (Figure 9). Together, these results point to a difference in the surface reference; they do not by themselves identify an inconsistency in ERA5-Land’s pressure adjustment or published orography.

S4 Reference-height uncertainty and sensitivity

MeteoSwiss corroboration

SwissMetNet supplies 10-min instantaneous pressure at published barometer height (QFE, prestas0) [13]. We use finite full-UTC-hour values in 2022–2024 at 138 stations with a published barometer height and at least 2160 usable hours. Published sea-level heights are used without a Swiss-to-EGM96 transformation. Source: MeteoSwiss.

At 24 matched stations (Figure 10), replacing only the listed GHCNh reference elevation with the published barometer height reduces median station |bias| from 6.0 to 3.0 m, close to 2.7 m using MeteoSwiss pressure. Only the height-only contrast holds pressure and ERA5 series fixed: GHCNh uses its selected year, whereas MeteoSwiss covers 2022–2024. This supports a metadata contribution at these sites, without identifying the cause of discrepancies elsewhere. Table 5 summarizes the complementary ground references.

Reference-plausibility screen

Removing the ERA5-residual-based station screen changes central errors less than their upper tails (Table 6). The step/noise-only alternative removes the offset criterion but keeps the step-change and frequent-gross-observation checks from S1. None of these flags identifies the cause of a residual. Screened values should therefore be read alongside the all-eligible comparison, rather than as unconditional conversion accuracy.

Flight weights and height-band coverage

Primary flight weights give each station equal total weight across all its retained levels; its contribution within a particular band therefore depends on vertical sampling. All 648 retained stations occupy distinct 2° cells, so equal cell and equal station weights are equivalent for this network. We compared equal station weights within bands, equal sounding weights within station–bands, and minimum coverage of 30 or 100 soundings per station–band. The corrected conversion retains the lowest flight-time-weighted median absolute error (Table 7), although height-specific upper tails vary (Table 8). Coverage thresholds change the contributing population; they do not establish more accurate references.

Biological flight target and height weights

The biological target is the flight-time height distribution of 203 tags from 25 species (34,580 represented flight hours) in the Master GeoLocator Data Package, version 2026.0 [14]. Inputs match the published checksums. We retain most-likely pressurepath records with finite tag and surface pressure and no discard label; non-integer stationary-period identifiers mark flight. Upstream classifications and pressurepaths are used as supplied, without uniformly reprocessing the tracks.

Table 9 gives the height and duration assumptions needed to reproduce the weights. Main-manuscript Figure 4c shows the resulting height distribution. Alternative flight-duration, low-height and equal-tag targets preserve the conversion ranking (Table 10). Equal-tag weighting gives each contributing tag the same total weight, whereas the primary target pools represented flight time; neither is a global sample of birds. The two-hour threshold is based on represented sampling intervals, rather than directly observed take-off and landing.

Removing the stationary pressure-offset adjustment, shifting all estimated heights by ±100 m, or changing the height formula on the subset with complete weather annotations also preserves the ranking. These stress tests do not supply uncertainty intervals or make the weights independent of the conversion assumptions. Full results, annotation coverage, species contributions and sampling cadence accompany the code [1].

Reference dependence

ERA5 assimilates conventional surface and upper-air observations [9]; we did not establish whether each evaluated station, variable and date was assimilated. GNSS archive membership does not establish independence. The terrain-matched archive comparison (Table 11) and nearby-station counts (Table 12) are descriptive checks only: similar errors across archives, or at isolated stations, cannot quantify assimilation influence. Reference-height uncertainty and the residual-based screen remain additional limitations.

Choice of ground observation year

The latest coverage-qualified year is selected by recency, without ranking years by ERA5 error. Selected-year station counts are 2022: 35; 2023: 40; 2024: 177; 2025: 404; 2026: 1327. Partial 2026 records have incomplete seasonal coverage. Table 13 compares the selected year with the latest qualifying completed year on the same screened stations. Each paired year must retain at least 183 reporting days and four distinct accepted hours per reporting day after ERA5 matching; the station screen is held fixed from the selected year.

Processing provenance, including the paired GHCNh–HadISD transition audit, source-specific QC composition and repeated-GNSS-hour check, is retained with the code [1]. The primary results use unique GNSS station-hours and source-aware pressure QC as specified in S1.

S5 Sensitivity to horizontal position

Design. We shift the ERA5/GPT3 query position, keeping pressure, time and radiosonde reference height fixed. The fixed-seed pilot samples ten IGRA2 stations across five climate zones and two terrain strata (<100 or \(\geq 100\) m sub-grid orography SD; six northern and four southern stations). Each supplies two eligible launches nearest mid-quarter per quarter of 2024, using the level nearest 2 km (within 1.7–2.3 km) and its surface record. Displacements are 0, 10, 25, 50, 100 and 200 km, with eight bearings at positive distances. Small shifts can select the same ERA5 cell; the standard atmosphere is location-independent.

Interpretation. Absolute altitude and surface-referenced flight height respond differently (Figure 11). The latter subtracts the surface error at the same displaced position and original surface-observation time. Small changes in pooled median error can conceal larger individual paired changes (Table 14). This fixed-height pilot does not establish a global location-error distribution or acceptable displacement radius, and excludes terrain-clearance uncertainty, balloon drift, moving anchors and rare weather extremes.
